title: EM4100 / EM4305 / T5577 — LF 125 kHz Chip Technical Encyclopedia (Read-Only, Writable, Emulator)
kicker: EM Microelectronic EM4100 / EM4305 / Atmel T5577 Reference
summary: The 125 kHz LF (low-frequency) RFID chip family is the bedrock of legacy access control — hotels, buildings, gates, car-park systems, pet microchips, and livestock tagging. EM4100 is the read-only, Manchester-encoded 40-bit-ID reference chip shipping since the early 1990s. EM4305 is its writable EEPROM cousin, still carrying the same air-interface compatibility. T5577 (originally Atmel, now part of Microchip) is the programmable 'universal LF emulator' that can be configured to impersonate EM4100, HID Prox, Indala, ioProx, AWID, and a dozen other proprietary LF formats. Together they cover the vast majority of deployed LF credentials worldwide.
heroPoints: 125 kHz LF — inductively-coupled RFID operating at the unlicensed LF ISM band. Short read range (2-10 cm), robust against water, human tissue, and most non-ferrous materials. Not suitable for metal surfaces without a ferrite backing. No meaningful crypto on any of these chips; LF security depends entirely on the downstream backend.

EM4100 vs EM4305 vs T5577 — EM4100 is read-only, factory-programmed, 40-bit ID, EM/H2/H3 encoded. EM4305 is EEPROM-writable while keeping EM4100 air-interface compatibility. T5577 is the programmable 'universal LF emulator' — configure it to emulate EM4100, HID Prox, Indala, ioProx, AWID, and most other common LF protocols.

Legacy-reader interoperability — every 125 kHz access-control reader shipped since ~1995 reads EM4100-encoded cards. T5577's killer feature is the ability to clone an existing legacy credential onto a programmable chip, enabling both pentest workflows and legitimate key-duplication services. No other LF chip offers this level of format-flexibility.

sections.title: Family and part numbers
bullets: EM4100 — EM Microelectronic (Marin, Switzerland) LF chip family. 40-bit read-only factory-programmed ID. Variants include EM4102 (Manchester encoding, reference chip), EM4200 (newer silicon, Manchester, pin-compatible), EM4102-V41 (higher-endurance production run). Sold as wafer, die, or finished card / keyfob.

EM4200 — EM4100 successor with improved sensitivity and lower power consumption. 128-bit ID field but with the first 40 bits Manchester-encoded for legacy-reader backwards compatibility. Replaces EM4100 in most new production since 2018.

EM4305 — EM4100's EEPROM-writable sibling. 512 bits of user-writable memory plus password-protected sections. Can emulate EM4100 Manchester output, making it usable as a drop-in EM4100 replacement in locations that want writable cards for in-field provisioning.

Atmel T5577 — originally Atmel (now Microchip after 2016 acquisition) part number AT5577. Programmable LF emulator with 7 × 32-bit memory blocks (224 bits total) and configuration registers that determine output encoding, modulation, bit rate, and data payload. Can emulate EM4100, HID Prox (26-bit H10301 format), Indala ASP, Indala LogE, ioProx (Kantech), AWID, HITAG 1, HITAG 2 (partial), and a few other protocols.

HITAG 1 / HITAG 2 / HITAG S — NXP LF chips (formerly Philips Semiconductors) with 48-bit crypto authentication (HITAG 2) or Public-Key crypto (HITAG S with AES-128). Used in automotive-immobilizer and some European access-control systems. Out of scope for this guide's main focus but noted as the 'secured LF' alternative.

Counterfeit watch — 'EM4100-compatible' generic LF cards often ship as T5577 chips configured for EM4100 emulation rather than actual EM4102 silicon. For most access-control deployments this is indistinguishable. For pet/livestock ISO 11784/11785 compliance where the chip ID format is audited, insist on authentic EM4305 or ISO-compliant HDX/FDX-B silicon.

sections.title: Memory architecture — EM4100 (read-only)
bullets: Total memory — 64 bits, factory-programmed in a 2-line metal mask. Structure: 9 bits header (all 1s) + 10 bytes ID in Manchester/H2/H3 encoding (44 bits for ID + parity) + 1 stop bit. Total per-broadcast frame = 64 bits.
ID field structure — 40 bits. Bytes 1-2 = customer/version code (8 bits). Bytes 3-5 = unique ID (32 bits). This is the 'tag ID' reported by LF readers; access-control backends whitelist these.

Encoding — Manchester, Biphase (H2), or PSK1 depending on chip variant. Manchester is the dominant encoding for EM4100; at 125 kHz carrier with 64-bit ID and 64-clock modulation, full broadcast frame takes ~33 ms.
No authentication, no writable memory — the chip simply broadcasts its ID continuously whenever it is in an LF reader's inductive field. Nothing else.

UID uniqueness — factory-guaranteed uniqueness within the EM production run. Across global installed-base, the 40-bit ID space (1.1 trillion) is theoretically adequate but collision has been reported within budget-card production batches from non-EM clone houses.

Lifetime — no wear-out mechanism; the ROM is mask-programmed silicon. Card lifetime is limited by physical damage to the antenna coil, not the chip. Typical PVC cards rated ≥ 10 years outdoor, ≥ 20 years indoor.

sections.title: Memory architecture — EM4305 and T5577 (writable)
bullets: EM4305 memory — 512 bits organized as 16 × 32-bit blocks. Block 0 = chip-info/configuration. Blocks 1-13 = user memory. Blocks 14-15 = passwords and protect bits. Supports 64-bit and 96-bit ID formats plus custom user data.

EM4305 write — programmable via LF field modulation. The reader sends WRITE commands by modulating the LF field; the chip decodes and writes the specified block to its EEPROM. Write latency ~5-20 ms per block.

EM4305 password protection — optional 32-bit password required for write operations. Without the password, cards can be read but not modified. Password can be set at personalization time and locked thereafter.

T5577 memory — 7 × 32-bit blocks (224 bits), plus configuration registers. Block 0 = config (modulation type, bit rate, password flag, max block). Blocks 1-7 = user data / emulated-credential payload. Configuration determines how the chip broadcasts the blocks.

T5577 modulation modes — supports Manchester, Biphase, PSK1, PSK2, PSK3, FSK1, FSK2, FSK1a, FSK2a encoding. Combined with programmable bit rate (RF/8, RF/16, RF/32, RF/40, RF/50, RF/64, RF/100, RF/128), this covers the output formats of most deployed LF protocols.

T5577 password — optional 32-bit password for write operations. When enabled, writes require a PASSWORD command preceding the WRITE. Unsetting the password flag once set requires writing a 'password-off' value while knowing the current password.
T5577 endurance — 100,000 write cycles per block. Data retention ≥ 10 years. More than adequate for issuance-and-forget access-control cards.

sections.title: Air interface and RF characteristics
bullets: Carrier frequency — 125 kHz (some chips support 134.2 kHz for ISO 11784/11785 animal-ID compliance — EM4305 supports this mode). LF ISM unlicensed globally.

Coupling mechanism — inductive coupling (near-field magnetic). The reader's antenna coil generates an oscillating magnetic field; the card's coil receives it, rectifies for power, and modulates its load to transmit data. Range is short (2-10 cm) because near-field strength decays as 1/r³.

Power budget — LF cards require substantially more reader power than HF 13.56 MHz cards (roughly 10-100× the inductive-coupling power density at the card). This is why LF reader antennas are physically larger than HF equivalents.

Read range by form factor — ID-1 card (86 × 54 mm, 3-turn coil): 8-10 cm on a quality reader. Keyfob (30 mm round, 30-turn coil): 4-6 cm. Glass-tag (12 × 2 mm, tightly wound coil): 1-2 cm. Animal microchip: in-body 0.5-2 cm.

Interference and read reliability — LF is robust against water, wet fur, fabric, and human tissue. Poor on metal (field cancellation at the surface) unless a ferrite spacer is used. Electromagnetic interference from motors, switching power supplies, and LED drivers can introduce read errors, but LF is generally less susceptible than HF.

Standards — EM4100 / EM4305 have no ISO standard per se; they are de-facto references. ISO/IEC 18000-2 is the 'formal' LF RFID air-interface standard and specifies Type A (active comms) and Type B (passive polling) protocols. Animal RFID is governed by ISO 11784/11785 (128-bit ID + FDX-B or HDX encoding).

sections.title: Programming and cloning T5577
bullets: T5577 programming hardware — Proxmark3 (open-source LF/HF reader-writer platform) is the reference tool. Commercial alternatives include RFIDeas RF IDEAS pcProx series, Identiv SCL3711, and various Chinese keyfob duplicators. All implement the standard T5577 WRITE protocol.

Cloning an EM4100 onto T5577 — (1) read the source EM4100 to recover the 40-bit ID. (2) set T5577 block 0 to config_word corresponding to Manchester encoding, RF/64 bit rate, max_block = 2. (3) write the 40-bit ID (with format bits) into block 1. (4) verify by reading back; the T5577 now broadcasts as an EM4100 clone.

Cloning HID Prox 26-bit — HID H10301 format is 26 bits: 1 parity + 8 facility code + 16 card number + 1 parity. On T5577: block 0 config_word for FSK2a, RF/50 bit rate, max_block = 2. Blocks 1-2 hold the 26-bit HID preamble + payload + sentinel bits.

Legitimate use cases — locksmiths offering key-duplication services, access-control integrators migrating legacy LF installations to new credential technologies, facility-management teams maintaining their own spares. Most of these workflows have been legal for decades.

Pentest use cases — red-team engagements assessing the threat model of LF-based physical security. Since LF credentials have no authentication, any LF card in field read range can be cloned in minutes with ~€100 of hardware. Treat LF access tokens as secrets protected only by physical proximity.

Operational hardening for LF installations — if replacing a legacy LF fleet is infeasible, harden the downstream: turnstile + security camera per entry point, facility-wide single-sign-on with second factor for sensitive zones, LF audit-log correlation with other sensors (CCTV, motion, network).

sections.title: Commercial deployments and application fit
bullets: Hotel key cards (legacy) — LF was dominant 1995-2010 for hotel locks. Largely displaced by HF 13.56 MHz from 2005 onwards and by BLE/mobile-credential from 2018 onwards. Residual LF fleet exists in budget hotel chains globally.

Office and corporate access control — HID Prox (26-bit and 37-bit formats) on T5577-compatible cards is the second-largest US corporate-access-control segment after HID iCLASS. Dozens of millions of active credentials globally; replacement cycle is slow because new credentials must be compatible with the installed reader base.

Car-park and gate access — single-family residential gates, apartment-building garages, industrial-site gates. LF's proximity-based convenience and short read range (user has to touch the reader) fits the human-factor model. EM4100 or EM4305 dominate in new residential deployments.

Pet and livestock identification — ISO 11784/11785-compliant FDX-B chips (HDX at 134.2 kHz is the ISO default for new implantable chips). EM4305 supports this mode; dedicated chips like HITAG S 256 are also used. Implantable glass-tag form factor, ~12 × 2 mm.

Car-wash, gym, printer — low-value-per-use tokens where UID-only authorization is sufficient. EM4100 cards and keyfobs cost ~€0.08-0.15 each at volume; acceptable for scratch-off or monthly subscription use cases.

Where LF is NOT the right choice — payment, high-security building access, crypto-grade identification. Any application where cloning has meaningful cost. Also not suitable for long-range operations (>30 cm) where UHF is the only option, or metal-surface mounting where HF + ferrite is the primary choice.

Migration partners — the modern LF successor is MIFARE Plus / DESFire EV3 (HF 13.56 MHz with AES). Many installed LF readers are replaced with dual-technology HF+LF readers that read legacy credentials during a transition window, then the LF side is disabled once all credentials have been reissued.

sections.title: ISO and manufacturer reference documents
bullets: EM Microelectronic EM4100 / EM4102 datasheet — the canonical reference. Memory map, encoding specification, electrical characterization.
EM Microelectronic EM4305 datasheet — describes write protocol, password structure, and multi-mode emulation (EM4100-compatible output + 134.2 kHz animal mode).
Microchip T5577 datasheet (legacy Atmel) — config word bitfield definitions, modulation-mode table, write command timing.
ISO/IEC 18000-2:2009 — formal LF RFID air-interface standard. Less commercially relevant than EM's de-facto standards but referenced in government and enterprise procurements.
ISO 11784 / 11785 — animal RFID identification standard. 134.2 kHz, 128-bit ID, FDX-B or HDX encoding. Compulsory for pet and livestock identification in most jurisdictions.
Proxmark3 community wiki — practical reference for T5577 programming, LF protocol reverse engineering, and legacy-credential cloning procedures.

faq.question: Is EM4100 secure enough for building access control?
faq.answer: No. EM4100 broadcasts its 40-bit ID without authentication whenever it enters an LF reader's field. Any LF-capable reader (including the ~€100 Proxmark3 and various ~€30 Chinese keyfob duplicators) can clone the card in seconds. For low-consequence deployments (gym, parking, printer) this is acceptable. For anything securing valuables or personal safety, migrate to HF 13.56 MHz with AES authentication (MIFARE Plus / DESFire EV3) or mobile-credential BLE.

faq.question: What's the practical difference between EM4305 and T5577 in a deployment?
faq.answer: EM4305 has EM4100 air-interface compatibility only, plus write capability and password protection. T5577 can emulate EM4100, HID Prox, Indala, AWID, ioProx, and most other legacy LF formats, making it the go-to chip for cloning and for universal-credential products that must work with multiple legacy reader fleets. If you only need EM4100 compatibility plus writes, EM4305 is slightly cheaper; if you need format flexibility, T5577 is the clear choice.

faq.question: Can I use EM4305 for pet microchips?
faq.answer: Partially. EM4305 supports 134.2 kHz operation and can be configured for ISO 11784/11785 FDX-B encoding, so technically yes. However, authorized pet-microchip silicon is typically ordered from vendors with veterinary-ISO certification (e.g., HITAG S 256 in a glass-tag form factor). For commercial pet-implant supply, source through an ISO-certified supply chain rather than repurposing bare EM4305 silicon.

faq.question: How far can a 125 kHz LF card be read?
faq.answer: Typically 2-10 cm for consumer readers. Specialized long-range LF portal readers (with large antenna loops, usually 30-50 cm diameter) can reach 30-60 cm, but at correspondingly larger physical footprint. LF fundamentally cannot match HF's bore-through range or UHF's multi-meter range; it is a proximity technology. For reads beyond 10 cm, pick HF + NFC or UHF depending on use case.

faq.question: Why does the industry still use LF when HF and UHF are more capable?
faq.answer: Installed base. The HID Prox, EM4100, and Indala formats have been deployed across tens of millions of doors and hundreds of thousands of facilities since the mid-1990s. Replacing a building's reader fleet is capital-intensive; LF credentials ship at ~€0.10 versus HF at ~€0.30 + the reader-fleet capex. New greenfield installations overwhelmingly choose HF or mobile-credential; replacement cycles on existing LF installations measure in decades.

faq.question: Can an NFC phone read 125 kHz LF cards?
faq.answer: No. NFC phones use HF 13.56 MHz exclusively. There is no commodity phone hardware for 125 kHz LF; some Android phones with external USB-OTG LF reader dongles can read LF, but this is specialist equipment. For phone-readable LF-equivalents, provide a dual-frequency card (125 kHz LF for legacy reader + 13.56 MHz HF for phone tap) or migrate fully to HF.

faq.question: What are the signs that an LF card I bought is fake or non-compliant?
faq.answer: Fake EM4100 often ships as T5577 emulating EM4100. Functional difference: T5577 responds to WRITE commands while EM4100 does not. A legitimate EM4100 will silently ignore WRITE; a T5577-masquerading card will accept writes and change its ID. For pet-microchip ISO 11784/11785 applications where the chip ID format is audited, insist on ISO-certified supply chain from a named vendor; for general access-control applications, the functional equivalence is usually acceptable.
